Description: I think I can safely say that any dunk in the ocean leaves you feeling so refreshed and energised, and that was certainly the case this morning. I’ve been on the road a fair bit lately, and my morning starts have meant that I haven’t been able to get to the water and have a swim, but that was different today. I say it was funny because as my friend and I hit the sand/water interface, we both looked at each other and thought, “it’s not too cold.” Diving in and splashing around for a little while, our next words were “Well…. actually, it’s very cold!” And that right there is what makes it worthwhile - the moment where you get pushed out of your comfort zone and all your senses get invigorated.

Title: Costa's Corner .... 16th September 2022 - Gardening Australia
Description:
There have been so many fantastic events going on around the country this week and I have been incredibly fortunate to be a part of a generous serve of them. After the wonderful Green Day and school visits and community Green Day in Mudgee, I had the opportunity to head out to central Victoria to celebrate all things daffodil at the Kyneton Daffodil Festival. This was small town community buzz at its best and I can’t tell you how much of a feeling it was to be there early in the morning, doing what we needed to do for filming and to slowly see the main street fill up with onlookers for the parade.
Our crew did a fantastic job to get all the footage we needed as well as a chat with the incredible powerhouse and stalwart  behind the festival  Marg Derricot. She embodies everything about a generation of community builders who turn up and represent and put in above and beyond for the good of the local community. Marg and her husband Eric have been bringing all the threads of that festival together for decades.

Title: Costa's Corner .... 3rd June 2022 - Gardening Australia
Description: Banksias have been a part of my entire life. Growing up close to the coast here in Sydney, they are just a participant of every landscape. Any open space or park, or the bush reserves along the coastline, are all populated with typical Banksia species associated with what is referred to around the city, harbour and eastern suburbs of Sydney as ‘Banksia scrub.’ They are purely and simply an iconic coastal species that are so etched into my mind (and equally into the balls of my feet from having trodden on them running around the streets, or when walking up the beach access ways, before the obligatory beachside car park. One of the things that I absolutely adore about the Banksia is the trunk, particularly when you get the chance to be up close and personal with an older tree. The gnarly and knobbly texture is something that has captured my imagination for as long as I can remember.

Title: Costa's Corner .... 27th May 2022 - Gardening Australia
Description: May is drawing to a close and we are heading into the sixth (and halfway) month of the year. Hello hello! Did I just imagine that or what? Although, there is one thing that can break you out of your imagination of the cooler months of the year, and that’s coming down to Melbourne, travelling to Ballarat and then getting out of your mode of transport. It’s at that point that you realise that we are into the winter in the south. It’s always one of those great moments that I enjoy, and I suppose I would compare the feeling to a similar one that I get when you cross the mountains west of Sydney and step out of the vehicle in a place like Lithgow. Ballarat and Lithgow. Ballarat and Lithgow can cut you to the bone. And it’s not a bad thing, it’s just their thing at this time of the year and I respect it, but they always catch me out and usually underprepared! I reckon we all have a go-to icebox destination that always catches us out.

Title: Costa's Corner .... 18th March 2022 - Gardening Australia
Description: I grew up around flowers because of the love my grandparents had for them. My grandfather not only grew them for my grandmother he grew them with my grandmother and there was nothing they both loved more than asking you to look at a particular bloom, but better still to stick your face inside one and smell it. Thinking about this as I write reminds me of the fragrances, the sounds and the actions that they used to share simply because they were predictable about it. They wanted to lead you to the flowers in the garden or to a vase in the house that had been used to arrange them. And I suppose because of this I never saw flowers and floristry as the stereotypical thing that girls were given. My grandmother grew and gave as good as she got and then some. And my grandfather grew them and shared them with the same passion and vigour and zest and common love. The lines in the garden melted together between those two and I suppose because of that I’ve never seen any aspect of gardening as being delineated or the domain of one group or the other. They really were collective about it all.

Title: Costa's Corner.... 5th November 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description:
Here’s a big big shout out to everyone who has been involved in any of the wonderful citizen science projects that have been taking place in communities all around the country. You, me, everybody who has stepped up and decided to contribute toward the very valuable and inclusive practice of citizen science. You are really opening the door to a layer of community learning that I believe will grow exponentially as this decade of the 2020’s progresses. Community knowledge and information sharing is incredibly powerful. The captured observations made by individuals in both the family and community context, holds real gravity and respect. There is something very special about local truths, where communities and the individuals within them are the custodians of the facts - the facts of nature. First Nations people have been custodians of the facts and have shared information intergenerationally over thousands of years. Citizen science is similarly this community connected observation and recording - with just a slightly new name to fit the times.

So when I look at some of the events that took place over the last two weeks under the banner of citizen science, I can fully appreciate how and why these contemporary events are getting attention and momentum. Whether it is the Great Southern BioBlitz and going out and recording any life you see in your neighbourhood, or whether it is something like Water Night and not using your tap for 12 hours to see just how water fits into our daily consciousness, these projects share the same community building and sharing. Then throw in the Aussie Backyard Bird Count and you can start to see the pattern that I'm talking about. There is a real magnetic attraction around citizen science projects because people want to contribute and feel a part of the solutions to the challenges that we face as a community moving forward. Understanding, respecting and sharing ways of being mindful around water, or taking the time to sit quietly and observe the birdlife living all around us in our ‘naturehoods’ - these little contributions to the broader collective add a lot more meaning and impact than we may tend to think they have.

Nature tells the truth. There is no 24hr news cycle where it switches and swaps from one camp to the next for the sake of a headline. Nature creates headlines because that is exactly what is happening, and this is the reality of the current moment or period. As gardeners, we connect with people and share our experiences. We share the truths we have learnt and gathered through our observations and those of others who have shared with us. We cut to the chase quite readily. Does it work? Did it work for you? What was the process? What were the results? Would you recommend it? All of these questions are constantly reverberating around our conversations about garden science.  When we meet and spend time with a specialist grower of bromeliads, or vegetables, or fruit trees, we are actually entering their laboratory of specialisation, a place of exchange and understanding. As land carers or bush regenerators, we are assessing, observing and interpreting our observations at a rate of knots as we move through an area or a specific landscape. listening, smelling and seeing the cues required to understand the place in the moment.  How exciting is it when you stop and consider the daily transfer of knowledge and information and how important we all are as valuable cogs within the community wheel of fact transfer? Call it common sense, but captured observations really are the currency with which we build culture and create pathways of significance and prosperity by managing and helping to regenerate natures abundance.

Let me explain what I am bantering about with a firsthand example from last week. I was doing my daily bird count on Friday morning, I saw 97 birds from a mix of 9 different species. How amazing is that, for right in the heart of Sydney in Bondi? Anyway, on Sunday morning I decided to continue my daily count but this time I thought I’ll go and do my count in Centennial Park. I’m no sooner wandering alongside Lily Pond, when I hear my name called out and it was local bird specialist Steve Howard who I have met before at an event in Centennial Parklands some years ago. Anyway, he is like a community bird guide in the parklands and walks through every morning doing counts and observing bird behaviour. He knows what is going on because he has been doing it for more than 4 decades. This is a living and breathing example of the local truth. A custodian of the facts. Steve said how he has been observing the tawny frogmouths as they care for their new young ones and gestured that I follow him to a paperbark tree within about 10m of where we stood and there was the dad and three little ones perched on the melaleuca branch about 10m above us. What a privilege to be around this level of custodianship - this raw and true reflection of science being held and shared. These are the truths I believe citizen science nurtures and will showcase over the decades ahead like it always has - even if it has not been titled as such.

And it is not just about the facts and the truths, there is a comfort and a collective safety around the caring and sharing of information in this context. It is therapeutic. There is a social side to this science activity in its own right. The horticultural therapy that comes with being outside and the learning and sharing of the observations and knowledge is another aspect and benefit within it all. So as though this isn’t enough, having a week with bird counts and water nights and BioBlitz’s culminating in the Australian Citizen Science Conference, there is still more. The actual therapeutic benefits of being outside in nature and the bush is recognised as a valuable form of therapy known as Bush Adventure Therapy. You may or may not have heard of it, but there are a variety of elements that make up this field and it includes horticultural therapy and even equine therapy. And at a time when humans around the world are responding to threats that have had massive impacts on mental health, the importance of the outdoors and nature as a place of therapy is going to grow in importance. The Australian Association of Bush Adventure Therapy held its second National Symposium online this week. It brought together all those specialists involved with nature therapy as a practice, and as gardeners, we are all too aware of just how important our daily ecotherapy is to our physical, mental and emotional wellbeing.

As I look out the window this morning, I can smell the rain from yesterday and see the plants standing happily after nature’s thirst quencher. Don’t you just love that calm that comes the morning after rain? The birds are chirping after being undercover all day. Of course, nature can also leave behind some turbulence, and I must give a call out to all those in Melbourne who were impacted by the massive storm last week and are cleaning up from the damage that it caused.

Description: I am having such a flap of a week. It’s Bird Week! (You may have heard or seen my posts flapping away about the Aussie Backyard Bird Count.) So many people are getting involved with it each year, and as a Citizen Science Project, it simply goes from strength to strength because of you and me - amateur and/or budding twitchers, keen to take on the daily task of dedicating 20 minutes to standing or sitting still, either in the backyard at home, in the street, down at the park, at work or wherever you may be, and observing the environment to see what birdlife may swing by. It’s as simple as that, and I have been doing morning counts, but have also mixed it up and done some afternoon and early evening counts too. The time allotment of 20 minutes absolutely rockets by, and if you are using the app, it has a counter on it, so you know exactly how long until the 20 minutes is up. Title: Costa's Corner.... 15th October 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: I need to sing some praise out LOUD. I want to share with you some yarns about our Botanic Gardens and just how important the work they are doing really is. I know that when most people think about the Botanic Gardens, the initial thought is a relaxing afternoon on a picnic rug, a nice stroll around while waiting for an appointment, catching up with a friend… or maybe it's even the perfect destination for your daily exercise and run! These are all wonderful answers and are exactly what our Botanic Gardens are all about - for us to get out there and get in them. But there is another whole layer to our Botanic Gardens that many of us don't know very much about. Of course, for those of you that are volunteers at the many ‘Friends Of’ groups, the Botanic Gardens Groups are where people come together to help propagate plant material that then can be sold to raise more funds to do more research, then you will know already that there is a whole world of activity going on behind the scenes. They are actually living, breathing research organisations that are doing the most valuable plant research that is clearly focused on generations to come and being the custodians of the landscapes that we are.

Title: Costa's Corner.... 17th September 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: There is nothing I love more than appreciating the joys and nuances of age; those wonderful intergenerational divides that make life the interesting road that it is. The innocence and naivety of youth, juxtaposed with the experience and knowing of those with time, and many years, spent orbiting the sun. I love being around children. Some may call it ‘working with kids’.. or at least that’s what the form says when you are doing anything in a professional context with kids these days. But I call it hanging out and just being in the world in a different way. Then there are the elders (and I call them this because ‘seniors’ has a certain implication that doesn’t gel with me.) The term ‘elders’ is appreciative and open, whereas seniors tends to put our most experienced travellers on this planet into a box that is predominantly based around age and the general assumption that with age, you are in some ways diminished or diminishing. So, these are the two markers to frame my banter with you today. Our children and our elders. I consider them to be the most valuable of assets for those of us in-between to draw on, celebrate, nurture and of course, engage with.

Title: Costa's Corner.... 27th August 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: I’m sure you are all familiar with how much we talk about the therapeutic importance of gardens on the show. It’s that side of gardening that’s like our body’s autonomous systems; we are not thinking about and instructing our hearts next beat or our next breath - it just happens. And when it comes to the garden, plants and growing, our involvement is having a benefit on us even though we aren’t saying and thinking about as we go. It’s not like I’m proclaiming that each little seedling you plant will immediately lower your heart rate, clear your mind and induce a great sense of inner calm and content, but there’s an unmistakeable and totally priceless side effect of gardening that is the underlying addictive fix that brings us back day in and day out for more. And I can safely say that it’s not just confined to the daytime. I am certainly guilty as charged for arriving home in the evening, long after sunset and gone to check on the chickens to lock them up and then started to weed the garden beds that catch my eye or prune a few errant stems. The list goes on. As does the ongoing benefit of having such time out on a daily basis. It’s what makes us gardeners nod knowingly when someone says they had the best day in the patch today or that they have to get outside NOW because they’ve been at the desk or at work all day.

Title: Weeds - Gardening Australia
Description: Gardeners are no strangers to the concept of weeds – it might be a clump of bindi-eye that pop up in your lawn, oxalis between your pavers or an errant dandelion in your flower beds. And while these may be annoying, and a little inconvenient, they are often the only obvious exposure home gardeners have to an invasive plant. But the reality of weeds in Australia goes far beyond the fence line – in fact, 70% of Australia’s most damaging environmental and agricultural weeds have their origins as garden plants. The importance of knowing what we grow, and how it may impact the wider environment is something that all gardeners should have an understanding of.

Title: Costa's Corner.... 25th June 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: So many communities have been affected by bushfire recently and in the near past. For many individuals and families, the experience and loss associated with the bushfires is all too raw and still front of mind long after the news cycles have rolled onto the next headline and the associated reality. Life just doesn’t reset like a computer, or a news feed does. In putting together this week’s special episode, our researchers and producers have worked as carefully and thoughtfully as possible to illustrate just some of the stories that have come from the fires. We understand that the episode will bring to light some very difficult memories and emotions connected with the trauma and tragedy experienced. I know how hard the team has worked to carefully present the stories in a way that recognises the many emotions that may be triggered by sights, sounds, and locations visited. For those people for which it may be too much, we send you our love and our support in the knowledge that this is, and will remain, a deeply personal topic. We stand by your side and with you as your lives and the landscapes you call home slowly heal and regenerate. Thank you to all those of you who allowed us to film your stories. They are such valuable reminders and educational tools for generations to appreciate and learn from and for this we remain forever grateful.

Title: Costa's Corner.... 28th May 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: What a week it has been since I last put pen to paper. I was actually in Melbourne ahead of an International Composting Awareness Week event for the Boroondara Council who were celebrating the anniversary of their FOGO (Food Organics and Garden Organics collection). They asked me along to be part of the community composting celebration, and what a celebration it was with close to 350 adults and children turning up to not only celebrate but also to talk and learn more about compost! All credit to everyone who turned up on a Saturday afternoon with so much enthusiasm and interest to make an effort to be there and share their experiences; particularly the two families who got up on stage and outlined their 12 months on the FOGO road detailing the way it has impacted their approach to waste, recycling, and generally living more single use plastic and landfill free. Gardening has become more and more a staple across their day to day lives as a result. And what can I say about my two new besties at Camberwell Primary School, two brave young girls who are part of the Environmental Warrior Group but more importantly, are known and recognised as the environment ministers. It's so wonderful to hear this language being used around roles and responsibilities and what that means to step up and take public office. To take the stage in front of 350 people and clearly and articulately explain what their leadership group is doing when it comes to the school’s sustainability and climate change plan, was truly the kind of public statement that brings hope and the knowledge that our next generation is not only up to the task ahead, but they are taking it by the horns. So a big congratulations to everyone behind not just the FOGO program, but the resource recovery initiatives that have seen the Council take waste diversion from 48% to 68% in the last 12 months. Imagine if each council around the country diverted 20% more from landfill in the next 12 months. This is where the rubber is hitting the road and good people across the community are working together to do what they can do and influencing what they can. Exciting stuff.

Title: Costa's Corner....21st May 2021 - Gardening Australia
Description: Did you notice the numerics about today’s date - 21/5/21?  I always enjoy seeing numbers combining in different ways and this was a nice little pattern. Actually, to all the Costa’s and Helens out there in the world, may I wish you a happy name day. Most of you probably wouldn't realise that in Greek traditions, your name day is actually celebrated more than your birthday. Nice little cultural nuances that are always a joy to be a part of. So as a child, I enjoyed it very much because I had all the traditional trimmings of the birthday milestone with gifts and cake and carry on, but then there was this other date, May 21st, where I would get messages and phone calls and Greek sweets and cake and gifts from my grandparents and great aunts and uncles and other Greek family to say ‘Xpovia Polla’ which translates as ‘Years Many’. It’s the equivalent of saying ‘Many happy returns’, and in saying that, what better way to segue to my story for this week.

My grandparents loved plants. They had their collections, and I think I am safe to say that there are people in your life who have had collections. People who have had a passion for plants. Description: When our Website Producer, Melissa Baddeley, threw around the idea of me making a weekly contribution to your weekly newsletter, I was chuffed and excited about the possibility. From the first one that I wrote, I felt like it was a really nice chance to be able to have a chat to you about how things look through my lens on the world that is not just Gardening Australia on the telly, but behind the scenes aspects of the filming, the stories, the people, the production team, being out in the field and the challenges, the ups the downs, the perspectives that I have on the world that I engage with on a daily basis. It hasn’t been difficult - on the contrary, it has been an absolute treat. I haven’t had to think ‘What will I write about this week,’  - It’s been more of a case of what won’t I include in this week’s banter! I feel like it is this window or bridge where I can just have a chat with you about things that ring a bell in my world…stuff that gets my attention and holds together the threads of life that make waking up and doing what I do, the ‘Greek Salad’ that it is!

Description: Topiary Topiary Topiary! We’ve all had our experiences with topiary and seen peoples painstaking work in creating shapes out of plants. Either way, it has a place in the world of gardening whichever way you see it and I want to share a yarn with you about topiary that has a connection back to some of my earliest days of making TV stories when I was starting out with Costa’s Garden Odyssey.   This yarn is all about how horticulture can and does, make a difference on so many levels - in this case building an entire new civic status quo.  So here goes.

Title: Costa's Corner....9th October 2020 - Gardening Australia
Description: Some of you may have heard of it, but many probably haven’t. The Australian PlantBank. It is located within the grounds of the Australian Botanic Garden at Mt Annan in western Sydney. In a nutshell, it is the home of plant collection and storage in NSW. The seed and tissue culture collections are effectively a massive insurance policy against the extinction of native plants in the wild. It is the largest native plant conservation seedbank in Australia with over 10,000 collections and more than 100 million individual seeds stored. How’s that for a serious pantry! Some seeds that are harder to conserve are stored as tissue culture or placed in cryogenic cold storage. It may all seem a bit remote to you and I, but the work that all our botanic gardens do around the country is quite ‘unsung’ and ‘behind the scenes’. Biodiversity is the most valuable asset we have as a nation and as a planet, and the field trips taken by botanists to collect, record and store our broad range of plants is protecting the flora of our unique landscapes for our good and most importantly, the good of generations to come.

Title: Costa's Corner....25th September 2020 - Gardening Australia
Description: Here’s a question for you. What comes to mind when I say orchid? Cymbidium, phalaenopsis, Singapore, bush, native. Orchids have that real lean forward power associated with them. They capture your attention and really drag an awwweeee out of you when you see their incredible shapes colours and of course their sweet, sweet register of aromas. Do you remember your first orchid experience?  Who was the intrepid guide that introduced you to them? For me, it was all of my grandparents and that generation of great aunts and uncles in my childhood. They loved them, split them, shared them and simply adored showing anyone who stood still long enough their prized possessions when they were bursting with a spike or more. I can still see the sparkle of happiness and really deep joy that came from showing off what they had patiently waited for since the last flowering event. Memories are such a valuable possession and those connected to plants seem to have roots that drink from the water table of life and fuel your heart.

Title: Costa's Corner....14th August 2020 - Gardening Australia
Description: There’s absolutely no denying how valuable our gardens, parks, streetscapes and bushland has been for everyone over the last few months. As gardeners, we have already been exposed to the therapeutic aspect of gardening. That place for time out. The space where time seems to stop and we can get taken out of our day to day world and get immersed in nature. And there’s so many different scales of immersion. At the moment I am getting totally besotted with one of my indoor plants in the bathroom. It’s a Cissus alata ‘Ellen Danica’ - a climber whose every new tendril unfurling stops me in my tracks. I find myself gazing at the tendrils each time I see them and looking at their reflection in the mirror and talking to Ellen or Danica out aloud as I shave !!! (Well brush my teeth or wash my hands!)  It can be as simple as that. Then again, it can be pulling up after a day’s filming  or even at night when I get home late and thinking I’ll just go down and check on the worm farms , see if there are any new Share Waste scraps in the collection bins, pick some greens for the chickens and the list goes on.

Title: Costa's Corner....7th August - Gardening Australia
Description: There are so many ways we can look at weeds. Weeds are plants that can be found anywhere that humans are living or have been. Weeds are everyone’s responsibility because they are part of our world - be that locally where we live, regionally where we engage and nationally as a community. If we start to understand weeds and their habits, we can take steps to reduce their reach and impact on our landscapes. Weeds are plants that grow in places where they were not necessarily part of the natural landscape and because of this, they can become problematic as the new conditions support their growth and potential to become invasive. I suppose what I want to propose to you in Costa's Corner this week, is that there is a great opportunity for us to be flexible and receptive to change when it comes to our approach to weeds. And in the international year of plant health, where raising awareness around the importance of plants in every aspect of our day-to-day lives is the focus, the reality is that weeds are part and parcel of any landscape. Understanding the impact they have on the requisite balance that a local ecology has evolved over thousands of years then gives us the motivation, information and understanding to take action for the long term health of our landscapes.

Title: Costa's Corner....31st July - Gardening Australia
Description: The more I travel around Australia, the more I am totally captivated by our native plants. With each day that passes, it is becoming this wonderful obsession. An obsession I know will never ever be totally satisfied and complete! From the time I started to study native plants during my landscape architecture course, it dawned on me fairly early just how much more I had to learn. I had always been fascinated with our flora since my time on my godfather’s farm and all during my primary school years. The sandstone clifftops we used to explore near home during these years were always a wonderland of species that created such a picture book landscape. The bark and flowering cones of the local banksias and the fluorescent yellow of the coastal acacias would light up the calendar year with colour and tactile structure - from the cones to the brushes to the seed pods. They really were these other worldly shapes and forms that allowed the imagination to run wild.

Title: Costa's Corner - Gardening Australia
Description: Indoor plants. They have always captured people’s imagination…  such a valuable recruitment agent when it comes to getting people hooked on horticulture. Do you have a first plant that was special to you, that lived in your room? Sitting here, tapping away on the keyboard, I’m actually getting quite a few memories come flooding back; some from the more distant past and my childhood, then others to my days as a student, exploring new landscapes and plants during my landscape architecture studies. Then there were my travel chapters when I was living in Europe and seeing just how much people value their indoor plants, particularly in the cooler climates where snow and cold weather means any little bit of nature indoors is revered and nurtured as another family member.

Title: 2019 | SERIES 30 | Episode 02 - Gardening Australia
Description:
Hugh’s Good Life Garden: Sophie meets a gardener who’s leading the good life, keeping chooks, growing fruit and vegetables, and trying to be as self-sufficient as possible on his suburban block. 

FAQs – Yellow Eggplant | Lumpy Umbrella Tree | Lettuce in Summer: Jerry Coleby-Williams solves the mystery of the yellow eggplant, Jane Edmanson identifies brown lumps taking over an indoor plant and Josh Byrne explains why growing lettuce in summer can be a problem.  

Wild Play: Costa clambers, scrambles and balances his way around a Sydney garden that is purpose-built to encourage children to take risks and go wild! 

Ripper Idea – Drying Rack: As well as using fresh herbs, Millie likes to dry seasonal herbs for use over winter, so she makes a drying rack to hang in her garden shed. 

Late Tomatoes: If you missed the spring planting season for tomatoes, don’t worry – Josh shows how you can plant a quick-growing second crop now. 

Beechmont: Jane visits a gorgeous hill garden that is full of interesting plants, which inspires and supplies many of the cut flowers and foliage for one of Melbourne’s top florists. 

Future Proof: The summer harvest is still in full swing but Tino is already looking ahead and planting out a mixture of slow-growing and fast-harvest winter crops.  

My Garden Path: We meet horticulturist Andrew Price whose home garden on a busy road has been planted out for privacy with lots of colourful, interesting plants. 

Plant Profile – Crepe Myrtle: Sophie takes a closer look at one of the most versatile and rewarding small garden trees, Crepe Myrtle, which has something to offer in every season. 

Doing Time: Jerry explores St Helena Island in Moreton Bay, which was used as a prison settlement where convicts maintained one of the first farms in the region. 

Jobs for the Weekend: Seasonal advice on jobs to do in the garden this weekend.

Botanic Wetland: Sophie explores an urban waterway that has been rejuvenated to form the basis of a huge wetland and wildlife project in central Adelaide.

Title: 2018 | SERIES 29 | Episode 42 - Gardening Australia
Description:
Stonefields: Costa visits the home of acclaimed garden designer Paul Bangay, where he discovers a landscape inspired by a view and learns where Paul’s love of plants began.

Fresh Start: Millie’s vegie garden did well in its first year but is now having problems, so she looks for the culprit – and rebuilds the bed to solve the issue.

Surviving Summer: Jerry shares some tips on how to cope with summer heat in the garden, including working out when to water, how to keep crops happy and picking sun-smart plants in the first place. 

Kentia Kingdom: Jane is back on Lord Howe Island and discovers a nursery dedicated to growing Kentia palms, one of the world’s best-loved indoor plants.

Jobs for the Weekend: Seasonal advice on jobs to do in the garden this weekend.

Title: 2018 | SERIES 29 | Episode 41 - Gardening Australia
Description:
The Gardening Report: Costa calls in to visit 7.30 host Leigh Sales to see her new garden and offer some tips on how to solve problems facing a lot of inner-city gardeners.

Gardener of the Year Finalist – QLD: Keven and Amanda Corbett find joy sharing the work in in their Toowoomba garden, which combines a formal frontage with an artistically exuberant retreat.   

FAQs – Best colours for bees | Flowering basil | Transplanting Palms: Sophie suggests the best plants for attracting bees, Tino shows how to deal with basil that has gone to seed and Jerry has tips on transplanting palm trees.

Gardener of the Year Finalist – NSW: John Le Messurier has led generations of scouts and volunteers as they transformed a former coal mine near Newcastle into a native plant retreat full of wildlife. 

Gardener of the Year Finalist – SA: Brenton Roberts used lots of money-saving ideas to restore a heritage cottage and garden in the Adelaide Hills to a semi-formal wonderland for his family.

Top Tip – Tomato Potato Psyllid: Josh shows how to identify and deal with a plant pest newly discovered in Australia – Tomato Potato Psyllid.

Gardener of the Year Finalist  - WA: Troy Devereux loves the feel of Balinese gardens so much he has created his own tropical paradise in Perth, creating a haven full of colourful bromeliads, palms and other lush plants. 

Ripper Idea: Millie shows a smart way to make biodegradable seedling pots from newspaper, which can be planted directly into the garden.

Gardener of the Year Finalist – VIC: Athol and Denise Brand fell in love with a 2-hectare block near Morwell and mass-planted thousands of exotic trees and shrubs to create a garden for all seasons – then added a house. 

Jobs for the Weekend: Seasonal advice on jobs to do in the garden this weekend.

Description: A glimpse at Tonga's burgeoning vanilla industry. (1969)

Title: Papua New Guinea's first self-governing church inaugurated in Hanuabada - ABC International Development

Description: A group of young Tongans gather on a lawn to play music, sing and dance. (1961)
